cap: Cervical screening rules follow how slowly HPV lesions progress. As of 2025 the USPSTF recommends cytology alone every 3 years from 21 to 29, then primary HPV testing or a cotest every 5 years, or cytology every 3 years, from 30 to 65; the American Cancer Society (2020) starts primary HPV testing at 25. Screening stops after 65 with adequate negative results or after total hysterectomy for benign disease, but never for people with HIV. A screening test only sorts risk; colposcopy with biopsy diagnoses, and excision treats high-grade lesions. The 9-valent vaccine prevents infection but does not replace screening.
teach: Read the top grid as a decision by age and risk. The main labels give the USPSTF (2018) schedule; the added ACS 2020 lines show the other guideline, which starts primary HPV testing at 25 and does not screen younger people. Then read the middle row as the three separate jobs in cancer prevention: screen, diagnose, treat. A cervix that is still present keeps its transformation zone, so a supracervical hysterectomy does not end screening, while a total hysterectomy for benign disease does. Excision of the transformation zone treats precancer but removes supportive stroma, so conization carries the greatest risk of later cervical insufficiency. The vaccine contains L1 capsid protein only, so it cannot cause infection and cannot clear an existing one.
